meaning: The copula: it ends a sentence of the type “A is B”. 「だ」 is the plain form; 「です」 is the polite form.
connection: Noun / na-adjective stem + だ・です; i-adjective + です

senses.label: With nouns
senses.meaning: Follows a noun to say “A is B”. Use 「です」 with strangers and people above you; it sounds polite. Use 「だ」 with friends and family, or in writing.
senses.connection: Noun + です／だ (often in the pattern 「AはBです」)

senses.label: With na-adjectives
senses.meaning: Follows a na-adjective stem to describe a quality or state. Don't add 「な」 when it ends the sentence.
senses.connection: na-adjective stem + です／だ (✕静かなです)

senses.label: Polite i-adjectives
senses.meaning: An i-adjective can end a sentence on its own. Adding 「です」 only makes it polite. It never takes 「だ」.
senses.connection: i-adjective + です (✕高いだ)

notes: The final u of 「です」 is often devoiced, so it sounds like “des”.
In casual speech 「だ」 is often dropped, which sounds softer: 「きれい！」, 「学生？」.
Polite questions use 「ですか」. Plain questions don't use 「だか」; just drop 「だ」 and use rising intonation.
「だ」 can't follow an i-adjective: ✕「おいしいだ」. In plain speech, just say 「おいしい」.

daily.title: Introducing yourself
daily.description: Telling someone about yourself the first time you meet.
daily.example: Nice to meet you. I'm Wang. I'm from China.

daily.title: Chatting with friends
daily.description: Friends use the plain form and often add 「よ」 or 「ね」 at the end.
daily.example: Tomorrow's a day off, you know.

daily.title: Commenting on food
daily.description: Politely praising a dish at a restaurant.
daily.example: This ramen is delicious.

work.title: Giving your name on the phone
work.description: When you answer or make a call, say your company and your name first.
work.example: This is Yamada from ABC Trading.

work.title: Introducing a coworker to a client
work.description: When you introduce a colleague from your own company to a client, don't add 「さん」 after their name.
work.example: This is Suzuki from our sales department.

etymology: 「だ」 is generally thought to come from 「にてあり」 → 「であり」 → 「である」 → 「だ」. In Kansai dialects it became 「や」. 「です」 is said to be a contraction of 「でございます」 or 「であります」. It spread in speech from the late Edo period and became the standard polite form after the Meiji era.

similar.title: 〜だった・〜でした
similar.explanation: The past form of 「だ・です」. 「学生です」 means you are a student now; 「学生でした」 means you were one before.

similar.title: 〜じゃない・〜ではありません
similar.explanation: The negative of 「だ・です」: 「学生です」→「学生じゃありません」.

similar.title: 〜でしょう
similar.explanation: 「です」 states something firmly; 「でしょう」 is a guess, or checks with the listener: 「明日は雨でしょう」 (It will probably rain tomorrow).

meaning: The negative of nouns and na-adjectives: “is not …”. 「じゃない」 is casual; 「ではありません」 is polite and formal.
connection: Noun / na-adjective stem + じゃない・ではない・じゃありません・ではありません

senses.label: Plain negative
senses.meaning: Used with friends and family, or in writing. In speech people usually say 「じゃない」; in writing, 「ではない」.
senses.connection: Noun / na-adjective stem + じゃない／ではない

senses.label: Polite negative
senses.meaning: Used with people above you and strangers. 「ではありません」 is the most formal. 「じゃありません」 and 「じゃないです」 are a little more relaxed.
senses.connection: Noun / na-adjective stem + ではありません／じゃありません／じゃないです

senses.label: Past negative
senses.meaning: “Was not …” in the past. Plain: 「じゃなかった／ではなかった」. Polite: 「ではありませんでした」.
senses.connection: Noun / na-adjective stem + じゃなかった／ではありませんでした
examples: That shop wasn't famous back then.

notes: 「じゃ」 is the spoken contraction of 「では」. The meaning is the same; only the style differs.
i-adjectives don't use 「じゃない」: ✕「高いじゃない」. Say 「高くない」.
With rising intonation, 「〜じゃない？」 means “isn't it …?” and checks with the listener. It can follow adjectives and verbs, as in 「いいじゃない？」. Here it is not a real negative.
The 「は」 in 「ではない」 is read wa.

daily.title: Clearing up a mix-up
daily.description: Politely correcting someone who has mistaken you for another person.
daily.example: Excuse me, I'm not Tanaka.

daily.title: Talking about your tastes
daily.description: Answering casually when a friend asks if you like something.
daily.example: I don't really like natto.

daily.title: Picking up the wrong thing
daily.description: Talking to yourself when you notice you took the wrong item.
daily.example: Huh? This isn't my bag.

work.title: Explaining in a meeting
work.description: Politely saying “no” in a meeting or an email.
work.example: This matter is not scheduled for this month.

work.title: Written reports
work.description: Reports and news articles use the written form 「ではない」.
work.example: This method is not necessarily safe.

etymology: 「では」 is the case particle 「で」 (from classical 「にて」) plus the topic particle 「は」. Adding 「ない」 or 「ありません」 makes it negative. 「じゃ」 is a spoken contraction of 「では」.

similar.title: 〜じゃなくて
similar.explanation: 「じゃなくて」 is the linking (te-) form of the negative, used for “not A but B”: 「これは塩じゃなくて砂糖です」.

similar.title: 〜くない
similar.explanation: i-adjectives use 「くない」 for the negative; only nouns and na-adjectives use 「じゃない」.

similar.title: 〜ない (verb negative)
similar.explanation: Verbs change directly to the nai-form (「行かない」); they don't use 「じゃない」.

meaning: The past form of 「だ・です」: “was …”. Also used when you suddenly remember something, or to check a fact with the listener.
connection: Noun / na-adjective stem + だった・でした

senses.label: Plain past
senses.meaning: Describes a past role, state, the weather and so on. Used between friends or in writing.
senses.connection: Noun / na-adjective stem + だった
examples: When I was a kid, I loved baseball.

senses.label: Polite past
senses.meaning: Used with people above you, strangers, or in formal situations. 「どうでしたか」 is the usual way to ask how something went.
senses.connection: Noun / na-adjective stem + でした

senses.label: Remembering / checking
senses.meaning: Used when something suddenly comes to mind, or to check information you already heard. It doesn't have to be about the past. Common forms: 「〜だった！」 and 「〜でしたっけ」.
senses.connection: Noun + だった／でしたっけ
examples: Oh, I have a test tomorrow!
Sorry, what was your name again?

notes: For i-adjectives, the past is 「かった」 and the polite past is 「かったです」: ✕「高いでした」, ✕「高かったでした」.
The polite past of verbs is 「ました」, not 「でした」.
「だったら」 means “if it is …”. It is a conditional.

daily.title: Talking about a trip
daily.description: Telling a friend how your trip went.
daily.example: Kyoto was really beautiful.

daily.title: Suddenly remembering
daily.description: Remembering today's plans before leaving home.
daily.example: Oh, right. Today is garbage day.

daily.title: Asking how something went
daily.description: Politely asking someone about their weekend.
daily.example: How was your weekend?

work.title: Reporting a result
work.description: Telling your boss what the other company said.
work.example: Their answer was “under consideration.”

work.title: Confirming a schedule
work.description: Checking a meeting time with a client.
work.example: Our meeting is next Monday, right?

etymology: 「だった」 is a contraction of 「で」 (a form of 「だ」) + 「あった」: であった→だった. 「でした」 is 「でし」 (a form of 「です」) + the past auxiliary 「た」.

similar.title: 〜だ・〜です
similar.explanation: The present form. 「学生です」: you are a student now. 「学生でした」: you were a student.

similar.title: 〜かった
similar.explanation: The past of i-adjectives. 「暑かったです」 ✓, 「暑いでした」 ✕.

similar.title: 〜た (verb past)
similar.explanation: The past form of verbs. Nouns and na-adjectives show the past with 「だった」.

meaning: The polite form of verbs (the masu-form). Changing the ending gives the affirmative, negative, past and past negative.
connection: Verb masu-stem + ます／ません／ました／ませんでした

senses.label: Affirmative: ます
senses.meaning: For habits, future actions and general facts. It is polite: use it with people above you, strangers and so on.
senses.connection: Verb masu-stem + ます (行く→行きます, 食べる→食べます, する→します)

senses.label: Negative: ません
senses.meaning: Says you don't do something, or won't do it.
senses.connection: Verb masu-stem + ません
examples: I'm not going to the office today.

senses.label: Past: ました
senses.meaning: Says you did something in the past, or have already done it.
senses.connection: Verb masu-stem + ました

senses.label: Past negative
senses.meaning: Says you didn't do something in the past.
senses.connection: Verb masu-stem + ませんでした
examples: I didn't eat breakfast this morning.

notes: How to form it: godan verbs change the final u-row sound to the i-row (書く→書き); ichidan verbs drop 「る」 (食べる→食べ); 「する→します」, 「来る→来ます」.
The u in 「ます」 is often devoiced, so it sounds like “mas”.
「ません」 is the present negative and can also mean “I won't”. For “didn't” in the past, use 「ませんでした」.
Friends don't usually use the masu-form. They use the plain form (行く／行かない／行った／行かなかった).

daily.title: Talking about hobbies
daily.description: Telling someone you just met about your habits.
daily.example: I often play tennis on weekends.

daily.title: At a convenience store
daily.description: Answering the clerk's question.
daily.example: I don't need a bag.

daily.title: Talking to a teacher
daily.description: Telling your teacher what you did.
daily.example: Professor, I handed in my report.

work.title: Reporting to your boss
work.description: Saying a task is finished.
work.example: I've already sent the documents.

work.title: Admitting something wasn't done
work.description: Honestly saying you didn't do it yesterday.
work.example: I'm sorry, I didn't check it yesterday.

etymology: 「ます」 is generally thought to come from the humble verb 「参らする（まいらする）」, through forms like 「まらする」 and 「まする」. It took its present shape in the Edo period. 「ません」 is 「ませ」 + the negative auxiliary 「ん（ぬ）」.

similar.title: 〜ない
similar.explanation: 「ない」 is the plain negative; 「ません」 is the polite negative: 「行かない」＝「行きません」.

similar.title: 〜た
similar.explanation: 「た」 is the plain past; 「ました」 is the polite past: 「行った」＝「行きました」.

similar.title: 〜ましょう
similar.explanation: 「ましょう」 is the volitional form of ます, meaning “let's …”. It is not a tense form.

similar.title: 〜ませんか
similar.explanation: It looks like a negative question, but it is really a polite invitation: 「一緒に行きませんか」 (Would you like to go together?).

title: 〜ない (verb negative)
meaning: The plain negative form of verbs: “don't / won't …”. It is also the base for many other patterns.
connection: Verb nai-form (godan: u-row → a-row + ない; ichidan: drop 「る」 + ない)

senses.label: Present negative
senses.meaning: Says you don't or won't do something, or that something doesn't happen. Used with friends and family, or in writing.
senses.connection: Godan: 書く→書かない; ichidan: 食べる→食べない; する→しない; 来る→こない
examples: I'm not going to school today.

senses.label: Past negative
senses.meaning: Says you didn't do something. Change 「ない」 to 「なかった」.
senses.connection: Verb nai-form → なかった (「ない」 conjugates like an i-adjective)

senses.label: Invitation: 〜ない？
senses.meaning: Said with rising intonation, 「〜ない？」 is a casual “Want to …?”. It is the plain version of 「〜ませんか」.
senses.connection: Verb nai-form + ? (rising intonation)
examples: Shall we take a short break?

notes: Godan verbs ending in 「う」 change it to 「わ」: 買う→買わない (✕買あない).
The negative of 「ある」 is just 「ない」 (✕あらない): 「お金がない」.
The nai-form of 「来る」 is read 「こない」 and written 「来ない」.
The polite equivalent is 「〜ません」: 「行かない」＝「行きません」.

daily.title: Turning down a friend
daily.description: Simply saying no when a friend offers you a snack.
daily.example: Thanks, but I don't want any right now.

daily.title: Inviting a classmate
daily.description: Casually asking a classmate after class.
daily.example: Want to go to karaoke after this?

daily.title: Complaining about your phone
daily.description: Complaining to your family that something is broken.
daily.example: My phone won't turn on.

work.title: Telling a close coworker
work.description: Casually telling a coworker you're close to about your plans.
work.example: No overtime today. I'm going home early.

work.title: Internal notes
work.description: Internal documents such as meeting minutes use the plain negative.
work.example: Company A will not take part in this meeting.

etymology: The negative auxiliary 「ない」 is thought to come from eastern Japanese dialects. It spread in Edo speech during the Edo period and replaced 「ぬ（ん）」, which was common around Kansai. Forms like 「行かん」 and 「知らん」 still survive in Kansai dialects.

similar.title: 〜ません
similar.explanation: The polite negative, used with people above you and strangers. It means the same as 「ない」.

similar.title: 〜ないで
similar.explanation: 「ないで」 means “without doing …”, or forms requests like 「〜ないでください」 (please don't …). It builds on the nai-form.

similar.title: 〜くない
similar.explanation: The negative of i-adjectives. 「ない」 itself also conjugates like an i-adjective: なかった, なくて.

title: 〜た (verb past)
meaning: The plain past form of verbs: “did …”. It also shows completion, discovery or remembering.
connection: Verb ta-form (formed like the te-form: change て／で to た／だ)

senses.label: Past
senses.meaning: An action or event in the past. Often used with time words like 「昨日」 and 「先週」.
senses.connection: 書く→書いた, 飲む→飲んだ, 食べる→食べた, する→した
examples: Yesterday I saw a movie with a friend.
Last week I went to Kyoto.

senses.label: Completion
senses.meaning: The action is already finished. Often used with 「もう」. A negative answer uses 「まだ〜ていない」 (not yet).
senses.connection: もう + verb ta-form

senses.label: Discovery / remembering
senses.meaning: Used when you find something you were looking for, or see something you were waiting for. It doesn't have to be in the past.
senses.connection: Verb ta-form (あった, 来た, いた, etc.)

notes: Memory rule: う・つ・る→った, む・ぶ・ぬ→んだ, く→いた, ぐ→いだ, す→した.
Exception: 「行く」 becomes 「行った」 (✕行いた).
The polite equivalent is 「〜ました」: 「行った」＝「行きました」.

daily.title: Talking about the weekend
daily.description: Friends use the plain form to talk about the past.
daily.example: Over the weekend I went to a new café.

daily.title: Finding something you lost
daily.description: Finally finding something after a long search.
daily.example: Found it! So that's where it was.

daily.title: Saying no to a meal
daily.description: When your family asks if you want to eat.
daily.example: I already ate, so I'm fine.

work.title: Checking with a coworker
work.description: Checking progress with a close coworker.
work.example: Did you send the email yet?

work.title: Meeting minutes
work.description: Meeting minutes describe what happened in the plain past.
work.example: The department manager explained the new plan.

etymology: 「た」 comes from the classical auxiliary 「たり」, itself a contraction of 「て」 + 「あり」, meaning “the state left after an action is complete”. Later 「たり」 was shortened to 「た」 and replaced classical past auxiliaries such as 「き」 and 「けり」.

similar.title: 〜ました
similar.explanation: The polite past. Same meaning as 「た」.

similar.title: 〜て
similar.explanation: The ta-form and te-form are made in exactly the same way; just change 「て／で」 to 「た／だ」.

similar.title: 〜もう〜た
similar.explanation: 「もう〜た」 stresses that something is “already done”. It is the typical pattern for the completion use.

title: 〜て (te-form: linking and sequence)
meaning: The te-form of a verb links several actions in order. It can also show manner, means or cause.

senses.label: Sequence of actions
senses.meaning: Links two or more actions in the order they happen, like “… and then …”. The tense comes from the last verb.
senses.connection: Verb te-form, verb te-form … + final verb
examples: I get up in the morning and wash my face.
I went home and made dinner.
I went to the department store and bought shoes.

senses.label: Manner / means
senses.meaning: The first part shows how, or by what means, you do the second action.
senses.connection: Verb te-form + 行く／来る etc. (歩いて行く, バスに乗って来る)
examples: I walk to school every day.
I found my way there with a map.

senses.label: Cause
senses.meaning: The first part is the cause of the second, like “…, so …”. The second part is usually a feeling or a result you can't control.
senses.connection: Verb te-form + feeling or state expressions (困る, びっくりする, 休む, etc.)
examples: I caught a cold, so I stayed home from school.
I was surprised to hear that news.

notes: te-form rules: う・つ・る→って, む・ぶ・ぬ→んで, く→いて, ぐ→いで, す→して. 「行く→行って」 is the exception.
The tense and politeness of the whole sentence come from the last verb: 「起きて、食べて、出かけました」.
For cause, the second part can't be a command, request or intention. Use 「から」 instead.
To stress “first A, and only then B”, use 「〜てから」.

daily.title: Describing your day
daily.description: Telling a friend your plans after school.
daily.example: When school's over, I go to my part-time job.

daily.title: Giving directions
daily.description: Telling someone how to get somewhere.
daily.example: Go straight and turn right at the second corner.

daily.title: Explaining why you're late
daily.description: Telling a friend why you were late.
daily.example: The train was delayed, so I ended up late.

work.title: Explaining steps
work.description: Showing a new coworker how to use the system.
work.example: Press this button, then enter your name.

work.title: Reporting your schedule
work.description: Telling your boss about your plans outside the office this afternoon.
work.example: This afternoon I'll visit clients and go straight home from there.

etymology: 「て」 comes from 「つ」, a classical auxiliary of completion, and later became a particle linking actions. Forms like 「書いて」 and 「読んで」 come from sound changes (onbin) that appeared from the Heian period on.

similar.title: 〜てから
similar.explanation: 「てから」 stresses doing B only after A is finished; plain 「て」 just links actions in order.

similar.title: 〜たり〜たりする
similar.explanation: 「たり」 lists a few examples with no fixed order; 「て」 links actions in the order they really happen.

similar.title: 〜から (cause / reason)
similar.explanation: For a cause, 「から」 can be followed by a command or request; 「て」 can only be followed by a factual result or a feeling.

title: 〜くない (i-adjective negative)
meaning: The negative of i-adjectives. Change the final 「い」 to 「くない」: “not …”.
connection: i-adjective stem + くない (いい→よくない)

senses.label: Plain negative
senses.meaning: Says something doesn't have a quality. Used with friends and family, or in writing.
senses.connection: Drop the 「い」 + くない (高い→高くない)

senses.label: Polite negative
senses.meaning: There are two polite forms. 「〜くないです」 is more conversational; 「〜くありません」 is more formal.
senses.connection: i-adjective stem + くないです／くありません
examples: It's not far from the station.

senses.label: Checking: 〜くない？
senses.meaning: With rising intonation, 「〜くない？」 means “Isn't it a bit …?”. Use it to check with the listener or ask them to agree.
senses.connection: i-adjective stem + くない? (rising intonation; often with 「ちょっと」)
examples: Isn't it a bit hot in this room?

notes: 「いい」 is irregular: its negative is 「よくない」 (✕いくない).
「〜くない」 itself conjugates like an i-adjective: past 「〜くなかった」, te-form 「〜くなくて」.
「きれい」 and 「有名」 are na-adjectives, so their negative is 「きれいじゃない」 (✕きれくない).
「〜たくない」 (don't want to) changes the same way, but it belongs to the 「〜たい」 pattern.

daily.title: Asking how spicy a dish is
daily.description: Asking the staff when you order.
daily.example: This isn't spicy, is it?

daily.title: Talking about the weather
daily.description: Chatting with a friend on the way out.
daily.example: It's not that cold today, is it?

daily.title: Showing a friend your room
daily.description: Modestly showing a friend your room.
daily.example: My room isn't very big, but it's clean.

work.title: Answering a client
work.description: Explaining to a client that the price isn't high.
work.example: This product isn't that expensive.

work.title: Evaluating a proposal
work.description: Gently pointing out a problem in a meeting.
work.example: I don't think this plan is very good.

etymology: 「〜くない」 is the adverbial form 「〜く」 of an i-adjective plus the negative adjective 「ない」. 「〜くありません」 is 「く」 + 「ありません」 (the polite negative of 「ある」).

similar.title: 〜じゃない
similar.explanation: The negative of nouns and na-adjectives. 「静かじゃない」 ✓, 「静かくない」 ✕.

similar.title: 〜くなかった
similar.explanation: The past of 「くない」: “was not …”.

similar.title: 〜くなる
similar.explanation: 「くなる」 shows change, “become …”; 「くない」 is the negative. Check what comes after 「く」.

title: 〜かった・〜くなかった (i-adjective past)
meaning: The past forms of i-adjectives. For the affirmative, change 「い」 to 「かった」; for the negative, use 「くなかった」.
connection: i-adjective stem + かった／くなかった (いい→よかった)

senses.label: Past affirmative
senses.meaning: A quality or feeling in the past. The plain form is used between friends or in writing.
senses.connection: Drop the 「い」 + かった (楽しい→楽しかった)

senses.label: Polite past
senses.meaning: For the polite form, add 「です」 after 「かった」. You can't say 「〜いでした」.
senses.connection: i-adjective stem + かったです

senses.label: Past negative
senses.meaning: “Was not …” in the past. Plain: 「〜くなかった」. Polite: 「〜くなかったです」 or 「〜くありませんでした」.
senses.connection: i-adjective stem + くなかった／くなかったです／くありませんでした

senses.label: よかった
senses.meaning: 「よかった」 is often used on its own to mean “Great!” or “Thank goodness!”. Use it when you feel relieved, or are happy for someone.
senses.connection: よかった／〜てよかった
examples: I'm glad I made it in time.

notes: The past of 「いい」 is 「よかった」 (✕いかった).
For the polite form, just add 「です」: 「高かったです」 ✓, 「高いでした」 ✕, 「高かったでした」 ✕.
Nouns and na-adjectives use 「だった／でした」 for the past: 「静かでした」.

daily.title: Back from a trip
daily.description: A friend asks how your trip was.
daily.example: Okinawa was so much fun!

daily.title: After a meal
daily.description: Thanking the person who cooked.
daily.example: Thank you for the meal. It was delicious.

daily.title: Finding something you lost
daily.description: Relieved after finding your wallet.
daily.example: I found my wallet. What a relief!

work.title: Reporting on a business trip
work.description: Telling your boss how the trip went.
work.example: Last week's business trip was very busy.

work.title: Project review
work.description: Explaining the results at a review meeting.
work.example: Sales this time were not very good.

etymology: 「かった」 is a contraction of 「く」 (the adverbial form) + 「あった」: 「高くあった」→「高かった」. In the same way, 「くなかった」 is 「く」 + 「なかった」.

similar.title: 〜だった・〜でした
similar.explanation: The past of nouns and na-adjectives. i-adjectives can't use 「でした」: ✕「寒いでした」.

similar.title: 〜くない
similar.explanation: The present negative. Change 「ない」 to 「なかった」 to get the past negative.

similar.title: 〜た (verb past)
similar.explanation: The past form of verbs. The 「かった」 of adjectives also ends in 「た」.

title: 〜くて・〜で (linking adjectives and nouns)
meaning: The te-form of adjectives and nouns. Used to list two or more qualities, or to show a cause.
connection: i-adjective stem + くて; na-adjective stem / noun + で

senses.label: Linking i-adjectives
senses.meaning: Change 「い」 to 「くて」 to link two or more qualities, like “… and …”.
senses.connection: i-adjective stem + くて (いい→よくて)
examples: This room is big and bright.
This place is cheap and tasty.

senses.label: Linking na-adjectives / nouns
senses.meaning: Add 「で」 after a na-adjective or noun to link to the next quality or clause.
senses.connection: na-adjective stem / noun + で
examples: This town is quiet and clean.
Mr. Tanaka is helpful and a very kind person.
My older brother is a doctor, and my older sister is a teacher.

senses.label: Cause
senses.meaning: The first part is a cause, like “…, so …”. The second part is usually a feeling or about being able / unable to do something.
senses.connection: くて／で + feeling or ability expressions (わからない, 買えない, 困る, etc.)
examples: This question is too hard. I don't get it.
It was too expensive, so I couldn't buy it.

notes: 「いい」 becomes 「よくて」 (✕いくて).
When listing, both qualities should point the same way (both good or both bad). If they contrast, use 「が／けど」: ✕「安くてまずい」→「安いけど、まずい」.
「〜くても」 and 「〜でも」 mean “even if …”. That is a different pattern.
For a cause, the second part can't be a command, request or intention. Use 「から」 then.

daily.title: Recommending a restaurant
daily.description: Telling a friend about a good place.
daily.example: That place is cheap, and the portions are big too.

daily.title: Introducing your family
daily.description: Talking about your family's jobs.
daily.example: My father is an office worker, and my mother is a nurse.

daily.title: Describing where you live
daily.description: Talking about your town.
daily.example: My town is small and quiet.

work.title: Presenting a product
work.description: Explaining a product's features to a client.
work.example: This product is light and durable.

work.title: Explaining a problem
work.description: Telling your boss you can't finish the work.
work.example: There's too much work, so I won't finish it today.

etymology: 「くて」 is the adverbial form 「く」 of an i-adjective + the linking particle 「て」. 「で」 is the linking form of the copula 「だ」, which comes from classical 「にて」.

similar.title: 〜て (verb te-form)
similar.explanation: The te-form of verbs. Adjectives and nouns use 「くて／で」 and link in a similar way.

similar.title: 〜じゃなくて
similar.explanation: 「じゃなくて」 is the negative linking form: “not A but B”.

similar.title: 〜けど
similar.explanation: When the two evaluations contrast, use 「けど」 or 「が」, not 「くて」.

title: 〜く・〜に (adjectives as adverbs)
meaning: Turns an adjective into an adverb that describes a verb. i-adjectives: 「い」→「く」. na-adjectives: stem + 「に」.
connection: i-adjective stem + く + verb; na-adjective stem + に + verb

senses.label: i-adjective + く
senses.meaning: Change 「い」 to 「く」 to describe how, or how much, an action is done.
senses.connection: i-adjective stem + く + verb (早い→早く起きる)
examples: I get up early every morning.
Please write your name in big letters.

senses.label: na-adjective + に
senses.meaning: Add 「に」 to a na-adjective stem to describe how an action is done.
senses.connection: na-adjective stem + に + verb (静か→静かに話す)
examples: Please speak quietly in the library.

senses.label: よく (from いい)
senses.meaning: The adverb form of 「いい」 is 「よく」. It has two meanings: “well, fully” and “often”.
senses.connection: よく + verb (よく寝る, よく行く)
examples: I come to this shop often.

notes: The adverb form of 「いい」 is 「よく」 (✕いく).
「きれい」 and 「有名」 are na-adjectives, so the adverb form is 「きれいに」 (✕きれく).
Followed by 「なる」 or 「する」, it shows change: 「早くなる」, 「静かにする」. See the related grammar.
「近く」, 「遠く」 and 「多く」 are also often used as nouns: 「近くの店」, 「多くの人」.

daily.title: Getting kids out of bed
daily.description: A parent hurrying a child in the morning.
daily.example: Get up, quick! You'll be late.

daily.title: At the hair salon
daily.description: Telling the hairdresser what you want.
daily.example: Please cut my bangs short.

daily.title: At the library
daily.description: Reminding a friend to keep it down.
daily.example: Keep quiet in here, okay?

work.title: Filling in a form
work.description: Asking a client to fill in their details.
work.example: Please write your name correctly.

work.title: Serving customers
work.description: Reminding a coworker how to treat customers.
work.example: Please explain things to customers carefully and politely.

etymology: 「く」 is the adverbial (continuative) form of i-adjectives, and 「に」 is that of na-adjectives (called 「形容動詞」 in traditional grammar). Both can describe verbs directly.

similar.title: 〜くなる・〜になる
similar.explanation: Followed by 「なる」, it means “become …”. This is the most common set use of the adverb form.

similar.title: 〜くて・〜で
similar.explanation: 「くて／で」 link to the next description or clause; 「く／に」 describe a verb.

similar.title: 〜な + noun
similar.explanation: To describe a noun, use 「な」 (静かな部屋); to describe a verb, use 「に」 (静かに話す).

title: 〜な + noun (na-adjectives before nouns)
meaning: When a na-adjective describes a noun, add 「な」 after the stem, then the noun.

senses.label: Describing nouns
senses.meaning: When a na-adjective comes before a noun, add 「な」 after the stem. Like in English, the adjective goes before the noun.
senses.connection: na-adjective stem + な + noun (静かな町, 有名な人)

senses.label: 大きな・小さな
senses.meaning: 「大きな」 and 「小さな」 look like na-adjectives, but they are pre-noun words (rentaishi) and can only come before nouns. They mean about the same as 「大きい」 and 「小さい」, with a slightly more emotional feel.
senses.connection: 大きな／小さな + noun (大きな家, 小さな声)
examples: There's a big tree in front of the station.
Please speak in a quiet voice.

notes: Don't add 「な」 at the end of a sentence: 「この町は静かです」 (✕静かなです).
「きれい」, 「嫌い」 and 「有名」 end in the sound 「い」, but they are na-adjectives: 「きれいな花」 (✕きれい花).
「同じ」 is an exception and goes straight before a noun: 「同じ本」 (✕同じな本).
A noun describing a noun uses 「の」: 「日本の車」. Only na-adjectives use 「な」.

daily.title: Talking about your hometown
daily.description: Telling a friend about where you're from.
daily.example: My country is famous for its beautiful sea.

daily.title: Asking about likes
daily.description: Asking a new friend what they like.
daily.example: Who's your favorite singer?

daily.title: Looking for an apartment
daily.description: Telling the real estate agent what you want.
daily.example: I'd like a quiet room close to the station.

work.title: Company notice
work.description: Flagging something important at the start of an email.
work.example: We have an important announcement.

work.title: Explaining a product
work.description: Telling a client about a product's strong points.
work.example: This app is easy to use with simple controls.

etymology: In traditional grammar, na-adjectives are called 「形容動詞」. The 「な」 before nouns comes from 「なる」, a form of the classical 「なり」 conjugation, which later lost its 「る」 (静かなる→静かな).

similar.title: 〜の (possession / describing)
similar.explanation: A noun describes a noun with 「の」 (日本の車); a na-adjective describes a noun with 「な」 (便利な車).

similar.title: 〜に (adjectives as adverbs)
similar.explanation: To describe a verb, na-adjectives use 「に」: 「静かに話す」.

similar.title: 〜 (verb plain form) + noun
similar.explanation: i-adjectives and the plain form of verbs go directly before nouns, with nothing added: 「高い本」, 「読んだ本」.

title: 〜は (topic)
meaning: Marks the topic of the sentence, “as for …”. It can also show contrast. It is written 「は」 but read wa.

senses.label: Marking the topic
senses.meaning: The word before 「は」 is the topic, and the rest of the sentence says something about it. The topic is usually already known to both speakers.
senses.connection: Noun + は + comment (AはBです)
examples: Tokyo is the capital of Japan.

senses.label: Contrast
senses.meaning: Puts two things side by side to show how they differ. Often 「Aは〜が、Bは〜」.
senses.connection: Noun + は〜が／けど、noun + は〜
examples: I eat meat, but I don't eat fish.
Weekdays are busy, but weekends are free.

senses.label: After other particles
senses.meaning: 「には」, 「では」, 「とは」 and so on turn a phrase with a particle into the topic, or add contrast.
senses.connection: Noun + に／で／と／へ + は
examples: There are three students in the classroom.
In Japan, cars drive on the left.

notes: As a particle it is written 「は」 and read 「わ」. Inside words (はな, はい) it is still read ha.
What comes after 「は」 is the main point of the sentence.
Question words can't take 「は」: ✕「誰は来ましたか」→「誰が来ましたか」.
「を」 and 「が」 are replaced by 「は」: 「本を読む」→「本は読む」. Other particles like 「に」 and 「で」 combine with it: 「には」, 「では」.

daily.title: Introducing yourself
daily.description: Giving your name and who you are when you first meet.
daily.example: I'm Li. I'm a university student.

daily.title: Saying what you drink
daily.description: Explaining what you drink at a dinner.
daily.example: I don't drink alcohol, but I do drink juice.

daily.title: Changing the subject
daily.description: Bringing up a new topic in a chat.
daily.example: By the way, what's the weather like tomorrow?

work.title: Opening a meeting
work.description: The chair announces today's topic.
work.example: Today's agenda is next year's budget.

work.title: Explaining rules
work.description: Telling new staff the company rules.
work.example: No eating or drinking in the meeting room.

etymology: 「は」 was a classical binding particle pronounced fa. Through a regular sound change (ハ行転呼) it came to be read wa, but the spelling 「は」 was kept. Its job is to pick out one element as the topic and say something about it.

similar.title: 〜が (subject)
similar.explanation: 「は」 marks a known topic, and the focus is on what follows; 「が」 marks the subject, and the focus is on the word before it. 「私は田中です」 introduces yourself; 「私が田中です」 stresses “I'm the one who's Tanaka”.

similar.title: 〜も
similar.explanation: 「も」 goes in the same place as 「は」 but means “also”: it adds something of the same kind.

similar.title: 〜は〜が〜
similar.explanation: In sentences like 「象は鼻が長い」 (Elephants have long trunks), 「は」 marks the overall topic and 「が」 marks the smaller subject.

title: 〜が (subject)
meaning: Marks the subject. Often used to describe what is happening right now, to bring in new information, or to stress “who exactly”.

senses.label: Describing what happens
senses.meaning: Describes something you see or hear, as it is. Often used with intransitive verbs or 「ある・いる」.
senses.connection: Noun + が + intransitive verb／ある・いる

senses.label: New information / emphasis
senses.meaning: When you answer “who” or “what”, 「が」 highlights the answer as new information. A question word that is the subject must take 「が」.
senses.connection: Question word / noun + が

senses.label: Subject inside a clause
senses.meaning: In clauses that describe nouns, and in clauses like 「〜とき」 or 「〜から」, the subject usually takes 「が」, not 「は」.
senses.connection: Noun + が + verb + noun / clause
examples: The food my mother made is delicious.
When my friend came, I was asleep.

notes: The object of likes, skills and wishes also takes 「が」, as in 「日本語がわかる」 and 「お茶が好き」. See the related grammar.
With 「は」, the focus is on what comes after; with 「が」, the focus is on the word before it.
「〜ですが、」 after a full sentence means “but”. It is not the subject marker.

daily.title: Seeing snow
daily.description: Telling your family what's happening outside.
daily.example: Oh, it's started snowing!

daily.title: Offering to pay
daily.description: Speaking up when everyone hesitates.
daily.example: Okay, I'll pay.

daily.title: Asking who made it
daily.description: Asking at a party who made the cake.
daily.example: Who made this cake?

work.title: Reporting a problem
work.description: Telling your boss about a sudden issue.
work.example: The system is showing an error.

work.title: Assigning tasks
work.description: Deciding who is in charge at a meeting.
work.example: Mr. Yamada will handle this matter.

etymology: 「が」 was originally a case particle showing possession; in 「我が国」 (our country) it works like 「の」. From the medieval period on it was gradually used to mark the subject, and it became the subject particle of modern Japanese.

similar.title: 〜は (topic)
similar.explanation: 「は」 marks the topic and talks about known things; 「が」 marks the subject and brings in new information.

similar.title: 〜が好き・〜が上手
similar.explanation: Here 「が」 marks what is liked or what someone is good at, not the one doing an action.

similar.title: 〜が (but)
similar.explanation: 「が」 after a full sentence means “but”. It looks the same as the subject 「が」 but means something different.

title: 〜が (but)
meaning: Comes after a clause and links two sentences with a contrast: “…, but …”. It is also used as a soft lead-in.
connection: Clause (plain or です・ます form) + が、 next clause

senses.label: Contrast
senses.meaning: Links two things that clash or don't match, like “…, but …”. More formal than 「けど」.
senses.connection: Plain form / です・ます form + が、
examples: This restaurant is expensive, but the food is good.
I'd like to go, but I don't have time.

senses.label: Soft lead-in
senses.meaning: No contrast here. It just softens your words before a request or a question.
senses.connection: すみませんが／失礼ですが／〜んですが + request / question
examples: Excuse me, where is the station?
Excuse me, may I ask your name?

senses.label: Trailing off
senses.meaning: The second half is left unsaid, and the sentence ends with 「〜が…」. This softens a request or shows hesitation, and leaves room for the listener to respond.
senses.connection: 〜んですが…／〜たいのですが…
examples: Um, I'd like to ask you something...

notes: 「が」 is more formal than 「けど」 and is common in writing and polite conversation.
Don't confuse it with the subject 「が」: the “but” 「が」 follows a complete sentence and is usually followed by a comma.
The lead-in use has no “but” meaning. In English it is often rendered as “Excuse me, …” or simply left out.

daily.title: Asking for directions
daily.description: Politely starting a conversation with a stranger.
daily.example: Excuse me, is there a convenience store near here?

daily.title: Declining gently
daily.description: Politely turning down a friend's invitation.
daily.example: I'd love to go, but tomorrow is a bit...

daily.title: Making a phone call
daily.description: Giving your name first when calling a friend's home.
daily.example: Hello, this is Sato. Is Kenta there?

work.title: Business email
work.description: Politely making a request in an email.
work.example: I'm sorry to trouble you when you're busy, but could you please check this?

work.title: Speaking in a meeting
work.description: Agreeing first, then raising a different view.
work.example: I think it's a good plan, but I'm a little worried about the cost.

etymology: The “but” 「が」 is generally thought to have grown out of the case particle 「が」. From the medieval period on, it came to be used at the end of a clause to link two sentences.

similar.title: 〜けど・〜けれども
similar.explanation: Same meaning. 「けど」 is casual, 「けれども」 is a little more formal, and 「が」 is mostly used in writing and polite speech.

similar.title: 〜でも (at the start: but)
similar.explanation: 「でも」 starts the second sentence; 「が」 comes at the end of the first: 「高いです。でも、おいしい」≈「高いですが、おいしい」.

similar.title: 〜しかし (at the start: however)
similar.explanation: 「しかし」 is a written-style word that starts a sentence. It sounds stiffer than 「が」.
